food.text: The Iraqi kitchen reached its peak during the Islamic Golden Age, when Baghdad served as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate from 750 to 1258. Many recipes from this medieval period survive today, still shaping Iraqi cuisine.
Kitab al-Tabikh, meaning The Book of Dishes, is the name of several medieval Arabic-language cookbooks. One of them was written in 1226 by Muhammad bin Hasan al-Baghdadi.
Arab traders controlled the flow of spices through the Levant to Venetian merchants bound for Europe. They held this route until 1090, when the rise of the Seljuk Turks disrupted their dominance.
Iraq's Muslims do not eat pork, because Sharia, Islamic law, forbids it.

Regional food traditions vary across Iraq: cooks in the north add pomegranate to dolma, stuffed vegetable dishes, while fish is a staple in the south. The center of the country is known for its rice dishes and sweets.
After the Seljuk Turks disrupted Arab control of the spice trade in 1090, the route through the Levant changed hands again. By 1453, the Ottoman Turks had regained control of this trade route.

Masgouf, a traditional Mesopotamian dish, was made from a whole freshwater fish from the Tigris, marinated in olive oil, salt, curcuma and tamarind, then roasted for hours with its skin left on. It was traditionally served garnished with lemon, chopped onions and tomatoes, alongside clay-oven flatbreads.

Mesopotamian stew, seasoned with leeks, onion, garlic, cassia, cumin, coriander, mint and dill, remained a mainstay of the region's cooking for millennia. Extant medieval Iraqi recipes, together with modern Iraqi cuisine, still attest to this long-unbroken tradition.
Iraqi cooking relies on staples such as olive oil, sesame oil, tamarind, vermicelli, tahini, honey, date syrup, yogurt and rose water, ingredients essential to the cuisine.

Among the dishes enjoyed in the region was zardah, a Persian rice dessert given a jelly-like consistency and dyed yellow with tea, sweetened with sugar and decorated with cinnamon, coconut and nuts. It was traditionally served on religious occasions such as Ramadan and Eid.

art.text: Krak des Chevaliers in Syria is considered one of the most important preserved medieval castles in the world. The Knights Hospitaller began rebuilding it in the 1140s, finishing before an earthquake damaged the castle in 1170.

The Great Mosque of Aleppo's current building mostly dates from the 11th through 14th centuries, though it was first built in the early 8th century. Its 45-meter minaret was constructed in 1090 by the city's chief Islamic judge, Abu'l Hasan Muhammad, and finished in 1094.

Mamluk architecture developed across Egypt, the Levant and the Hijaz during the Mamluk Sultanate, appearing in cities such as Damascus, Jerusalem, Aleppo and Tripoli. Major complexes combined a patron's mausoleum with a madrasa, mosque or other charitable functions in a single building.

Another earthquake struck the castle in 1202, after which it was remodeled into a concentric castle. A new outer wall built during this 13th-century phase gave Krak des Chevaliers the appearance it still has today.

In the second half of the 11th century the Mirdasids added a domed fountain to the mosque's courtyard. After a great fire destroyed the earlier Umayyad structure, the Zengid sultan Nur al-Din restored and expanded the Great Mosque of Aleppo in 1159.

After Sultan Qalawun captured Tripoli from the Crusaders in 1289, the Mamluks destroyed the old city and built a new one four kilometers inland. About 35 monuments from this Mamluk city, including mosques, madrasas and caravanserais, survive today.

Saladin's son al-Zahir al-Ghazi ruled Aleppo from 1193 to 1215 and rebuilt the citadel's entrance block in 1213. Under his rule the Citadel of Aleppo grew into a palatial city with palaces, baths, mosques and shrines.
The mosque suffered further destruction when the Mongols razed it in 1260 and burned it again in 1281. On the second occasion its minbar was taken by the Armenians of Sis.
Sultan Qalawun replaced the mosque's burnt-out mihrab in 1285. Later, Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, who reigned from 1293 to 1341, had a new minbar constructed for the Great Mosque of Aleppo.

Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil founded Tripoli's first congregational mosque, the Great Mosque of Tripoli, in either 1293 or 1294. Six madrasas, including al-Khayriyya Hasan and al-Qartawiyya, were later built around it.

Carved Kufic and naskhi inscriptions decorated the Great Mosque of Aleppo's minaret, alongside alternating bands of stylized ornament and muqarnas, a form of decorative vaulting. These decorations date from the Mamluk period, when the dynasty made repairs and alterations to the mosque.

Tripoli's Taynal Mosque, founded around 1336, has an unusual layout of two consecutive halls. The second hall, containing the mihrab, is reached through an ornate portal decorated with muqarnas and ablaq striped stonework.

war.text: In 1144 Imad ad-Din Zengi captured and sacked Edessa, the capital of the Crusader County of Edessa. Most of its inhabitants were allegedly slaughtered, together with the Latin archbishop. According to Matthew of Edessa, Zengi's forces killed many of the Edessenes.

The Mongols made their presence known in Edessa in 1244. In 1260 the Ilkhanate sent troops there, and the town voluntarily submitted to them. As a result, the people of Edessa were saved from being massacred by the Mongols.

The city of Amida, on the right bank of the Tigris, changed hands many times in the 13th century. The Ayyubids received it from their vassals the Artuqids in 1232, and the Mongolian Ilkhanate captured it in 1259.

Following the collapse of Byzantine control in Anatolia, Edessa passed to the Seljuq dynasty in 1087. An Armenian named Thoros then gained independence from the Turks in 1094. In 1098 the Crusaders established the County of Edessa there and kept the city until 1144.
Saladin, leader of the Ayyubid Sultanate, acquired Edessa from the Zengids in 1182. Under Ayyubid rule the city had a population of approximately 24,000.
In 1085 the Seljuk Turks captured the Amida region from the Kurdish Marwanids. They then settled many Turcomans in the region.

At the turn of the 11th century, Upper Mesopotamia came under a number of local dynasties: the Numayrids, the Mirdasids, and the Uqaylids. They persisted until the conquest of the region by the Seljuq Empire.

Our knowledge of the 1144 fall of Edessa, when most of the inhabitants were allegedly slaughtered, comes chiefly from the Armenian historian Matthew, who was born there. The city then had an Armenian population of 47,000. Steven Runciman wrote that the whole Christian population was driven into exile and the great city was left empty and desolate, and has never recovered to this day.
After the Ilkhanate captured Amida in 1259, the Ayyubids of Hasankeyf later took it back and ruled it. The city was then sacked by the Timurid Empire in 1394.
In 1146 the Crusaders briefly recaptured Edessa. They lost it again after only a few days.
The Sultanate of Rum took Edessa in June 1234. Sometime in late 1234 or 1235 the Ayyubid sultan Al-Kamil re-acquired it and then ordered the destruction of its Citadel.

literature.text: Al-Hariri of Basra wrote the Maqamat, a collection of some 50 stories in a mix of verse and literary prose. For more than eight centuries it has been regarded as one of the greatest treasures of Arabic literature, after the Quran and the pre-Islamic poetic canons.

Sebastian Brock calls the period from the seventh century to about 1300 the "Arab period" of Syriac literature. He describes it as an age of consolidation and compilation. It saw encyclopaedic forms of Syriac learning grow, and it culminated in the work of the thirteenth-century polymath Bar Hebraeus.

Gökböri, a leading emir of Saladin and ruler of Erbil, was the first Muslim ruler to publicly celebrate the birth of the prophet Muhammad. His ceremony included the recitation of poetry honouring Mawlid, the Prophet's Birthday. Earlier celebrations had been private observances or court processions, but Gökböri's were held in public, preceded by hunting parties and accompanied by lavish sacrifices.

When the Mongols approached, a book helped save a city. Sayyid Majd al-Din Muhammad ibn Tawus wrote a book titled Al-Bashara and presented it to Hulagu. Hulagu then restored local governance in the Euphrates region to Sayyid ibn Tawus and ensured the safety of Hillah.

Baghdad's House of Wisdom, established under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, attracted scholars from across the Muslim world to translate the classical knowledge of the known world into Arabic. The Islamic Golden Age it opened is said to have ended with the Mongol invasions, the collapse of the Abbasid caliphate and the Siege of Baghdad in 1258. In that year Hulagu Khan destroyed Baghdad and the House of Wisdom, which some see as the end of the Islamic Golden Age.

The Maqamat follows Abu Zayd of Saruj, a fictional traveler who deceives those around him with his skill in Arabic to earn rewards. It became extremely popular, with reports of seven hundred copies authorized by al-Hariri himself during his lifetime.

After the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate and the Mongol invasion of Baghdad, the scholars of Hillah knew the Mongols would bring catastrophe to any city they entered, with destruction, pillaging and violations of local laws. They met to decide what to do, among them Sheikh Yusuf ibn Ali ibn Muthahir al-Hilli, Sayyid Majd al-Din ibn Tawus and Ibn Abi al-Ghar al-Hilli. They agreed to send Hulagu Khan a letter expressing their willingness to submit to his authority, which preserved their city and its two holy shrines.
tags: Yusuf ibn Ali ibn Muthahir al-Hilli

literature.text: Because its scholars chose to submit, Hillah continued as a center of cultural and religious vitality. It safeguarded treasures of Islamic knowledge and literary heritage without the upheaval experienced by other cities in Iraq. After Baghdad fell, the Jalairid state chose Hillah as its capital around 1410.

Gökböri was a great patron of writers, poets, artists and scholars, whom he invited to Erbil. His vizier, the scholar Ibn al-Mustawfi, wrote a history of Erbil in four volumes. Gökböri also patronised the biographer and historian Ibn Khallikan.

Sometime between 1268 and 1277, Ibn al-Nafis wrote Theologus Autodidactus, an early Arabic novel that draws on his knowledge of biology, astronomy, cosmology and geology. Its final two chapters predict and scientifically explain the end of the world, doomsday, resurrection and afterlife, and its plot climaxes in a catastrophic doomsday apocalypse. The novel also argues that the Mongol invasions of Islamic lands were a divine punishment for the drinking of alcohol and for homosexuality among a small minority of Muslims at the time.

science.text: In 1206, the engineer al-Jazari, who worked at the Artuqid court in Mesopotamia, wrote The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, describing fifty mechanical inventions. Among them was his famous elephant clock, and he has since been called the father of robotics.
tags: Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices

science.text: The Iraqi scholar Ibn al-Haytham, later known as the father of modern optics, wrote his most influential work, the Book of Optics, between 1011 and 1021. In it, he proved that we see because light enters the eye, overturning the older belief that the eye itself sends out rays.

In Damascus, the astronomer Ibn al-Shatir worked as timekeeper at the Umayyad Mosque, tracking prayer times and the start of Ramadan. In 1371, he invented a new kind of sundial whose hour lines mark equal hours throughout the year, unlike older sundials whose hours changed length with the seasons.

The Nur al-Din Bimaristan, a hospital in Damascus, was built in 1154 for the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din. About ninety years later, in 1242, the physician Badr al-Din added an extension to the original building.

The Damascus physician Ibn al-Nafis was the first to correctly describe how blood flows from the heart through the lungs and back, known as pulmonary circulation. This overturned the theory of the ancient Greek physician Galen, which had gone unchallenged for centuries before him.

In the same 1206 book, al-Jazari described an early crankshaft, a wheel that turns continuous circular motion into the back-and-forth motion of a pump. He built this mechanism into a twin-cylinder water pump, a principle later central to machines such as the steam engine.

Between 1025 and 1028, Ibn al-Haytham wrote Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, criticizing contradictions he found in Ptolemy's Almagest, Planetary Hypotheses and Optics. He argued that devices like the equant, an imaginary mathematical point Ptolemy used to explain planetary motion, could not truly match how the heavens actually moved.

In Baghdad, the Al-Adudi Hospital was staffed by twenty-five specialists covering fields from optics to surgery and also trained new doctors. By 1184 it was described as being like an enormous palace in size.

Al-Jazari also described a camshaft in 1206, a rotating shaft fitted with cams that push and release moving parts. He used camshafts in his automata, in water-raising machines, and in devices such as his candle clock.

The Al-Adudi Hospital survived for centuries in Baghdad until it was destroyed in 1258, when the Mongol ruler Hulagu Khan besieged the city. Its loss ended one of the era's most prominent centers for training doctors.

politics.text: In 1258 the Mongol commander Hulagu marched on Baghdad, which fell after a brief siege in February. Its citizens were put to the sword in one of the bloodiest massacres in history. Hulagu ended the 500-year-old Abbasid dynasty by killing the caliph al-Musta'sim, an event traditionally viewed as signalling the end of the Islamic Golden Age.
politics.source_title: Mongol conquest of Persia and Mesopotamia

politics.text: Saladin founded the Sultanate of Egypt in 1171 after abolishing the Fatimid Caliphate. After his victory at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, most of the Crusader states fell to him, though the Crusaders reconquered the Syrian coastlands in the 1190s.

Created in 1127 as an Atabegate of the Seljuk Empire, the Zengid state was founded after the murder of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, atabeg of Mosul, when the Seljuks named Zengi as the new atabeg. Zengi was later assassinated by a slave in 1146. The state seized control of Fatimid Egypt in 1169, after Shirkuh lured the Fatimid vizier into an ambush and killed him. By 1174 it stretched from Tripoli to Hamadan and from Yemen to Sivas.

When Nur al-Din Arslan Shah I of Mosul was dying in 1211, his sons were still young. He promoted his army commander Badr al-Din Lu'lu' to atabeg as their protector. The son and two grandsons of Arslan Shah ruled as children until 1234, when Badr al-Din formally took over, possibly after assassinating the last Zengid emir, Nasir ad-Din Mahmud. A list of rulers in the article says flatly that Badr al-Din murdered Nasir ad-Din Mahmud in 1234. After 1243 Badr al-Din accepted Mongol suzerainty.

Most Numayrid emirs were Bedouin who avoided city life. They ruled from tribal encampments and left the administration of cities to their ghilman, or military slaves. An exception was Emir Mani' ibn Shabib, who reigned around 1044 to 1063 and lived inside Harran.

Nasr al-Dawla, the Marwanid ruler in Diyar Bakr, was a clever politician who steered between the Buyid emir Sultan al-Dawla, the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim and the emperor Basil II. He took Edessa in 1026, but the Byzantine general George Maniakes retook it in 1031.

In 1209 al-Adil I besieged Sinjar, but Nur al-Din Arslan Shah I of Mosul allied with Muzzafar al-Din Kukburi, ruler of Erbil, and resisted. Their truce let al-Adil keep his Sinjar conquests, while Arslan Shah agreed to recognize Ayyubid suzerainty on his coinage.

Under the Zengids, Syriac Christianity went through a "Syriac Renaissance" in which discriminatory rules against Christians were lifted, especially after the death of Nur al-Din Zengi in 1174. Important Christian manuscripts were made in Mosul, including a Gospel lectionary at the Mar Mattai Monastery around 1220.

In January 1059 al-Basasiri drove the Seljuqs from Baghdad, overthrew the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im and proclaimed Fatimid suzerainty over the city. Numayrid emir Mani' did not help him despite their formal alliance, and instead sheltered al-Qa'im's four-year-old grandson Uddat ad-Din in Harran, after the boy had been smuggled out of Baghdad. Al-Basasiri's reign lasted forty weeks and ended in 1060 with his defeat and execution by the Seljuqs.

In 1310 the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad restored Hama to the Ayyubids under the geographer and author Abu al-Fida. His son al-Afdal Muhammad eventually lost the favor of his Mamluk overlords and was removed in 1341, when Hama was formally placed under Mamluk rule.

In 1010 the Marwanid ruler Mumahhid al-Dawla was assassinated by his ghulam, Sharwin ibn Muhammad. Sharwin justified taking power with an ancient rule that whoever kills the ruler becomes his successor, but the rule and his reign were soon contested and he was overthrown.

philosophy.text: In Harran in Upper Mesopotamia, an astral religion held that a single transcendent power had delegated the governance of the world to the seven planets. Its central cult honoured the moon god Sin and was overlaid with Neoplatonic philosophy and Hermetic literature. Its public institutions declined sharply in the eleventh century, and its last temple was destroyed by 1081.

Arabic philosophical texts were translated into Latin, with the ideas passing to Europe via Al-Andalus, Sicily and the Crusader kingdoms in the Levant. This translation led to the transformation of almost all philosophical disciplines in the medieval Latin world. Muslim philosophers were especially influential in natural philosophy, psychology and metaphysics.
philosophy.source_title: Islamic world contributions to Medieval Europe

philosophy.text: Gökböri was a devout Sunni Muslim who built for the spiritual needs of his subjects. He founded a religious college in Erbil, the Dar al-Hadith al-Muzaffariya, in 1198, and also built sufi convents known as khanqah.

By 1184 the traveler Ibn Jubayr found no trace of the Harranian community or its cult. The Mongols had taken Harran in 1259 under Hulagu Khan, and its citadel was destroyed along with part of the city wall. When the Mongols withdrew in 1271, they deported the population to Mardin and other towns, destroyed the Friday Mosque and sealed the gates, leaving the city, in Ibn Shaddad's words, "an empty shell, but for the birds in their nests." By then Harranian Sabianism had already disappeared as an organized religion.

Hilal ibn al-Muhassin (969 to 1056) was the last of the Baghdad line of Sabians descended from Thabit. He converted to Islam around 1012. Ibn Khallikan preserved an account saying he did so late in life, on the advice of scholars, out of a desire for cultural refinement (adab).

Some scholars, notably Artur Rodziewicz, argue that a remnant of the Harranian tradition survived indirectly. In their view it was absorbed into Yazidism through the community around Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir at Lalish.

culture.text: Medieval writers in many traditions kept retelling the biblical Tower of Babel, set in Shinar in Lower Mesopotamia. The Jewish Kabbalistic work Bahir (1174) and the Syriac Book of the Bee (c. 1221) both mention 72 or 70 languages scattered from Babel.
The 14th-century traveler John Mandeville included an account of the Tower of Babel in his writings. He reported that its height had been 64 furlongs, according to the local inhabitants.

Dante Alighieri wrestled with the Tower of Babel and the language of Adam. In De vulgari eloquentia (1302–1305) he argued that the Adamic language was of divine origin and therefore unchangeable. In his Divine Comedy (c. 1308–1320) he changed his view and treated it as the product of Adam.

Giovanni Villani also dated the Tower of Babel precisely. He wrote that it was begun 700 years after the Flood and that they were 107 years working at it. He explained that men lived long in those times.

The Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum (c. 1284) gave its own count of the languages scattered from Babel: 22 for Shem, 31 for Ham and 17 for Japheth, a total of 70. It also claimed the tower was begun only 200 years after the Deluge, far earlier than Villani's date.

Dante's changed view had consequences for Hebrew. In the Divine Comedy he concluded that Hebrew could not be the language of Paradise but was a derivative of the language of Adam. He reasoned that the Hebrew name for God, El, must come from a different Adamic name, which he gave as I.
